stories.headline: Congress passes Russia sanctions bill, sends to Trump

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: The House passed the Russia sanctions bill 262-159 on Wednesday.
The Senate passed the bill 86-11 in August.
The legislation is formally named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
The bill honors the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who spent over a year negotiating it before his death in July.
The bill sanctions Russian officials, banks and financial institutions, and the 'shadow fleet' of tankers used to move Russian energy.
The bill reinserts sanctions on Iran's weapons and energy sectors.
The bill gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and natural gas (such as China and India).
The bill includes an exemption for countries importing less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports that have taken steps to reduce those imports.
Some provisions allow tariffs up to 500% on Russian imports.
Vote counts on Democratic support varied by outlet (reported as either 53 or 58 House Democrats voting yes).
A majority of Democrats opposed the bill.
Seven Republicans voted against the bill.
Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., broke with party leadership on a Tuesday procedural vote to advance the bill.
Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries issued a public rebuke to Golden and Perez.
Trump has said he will sign the bill into law.
The measure is described as the most significant congressional action against Russia since Trump returned to office.
Its passage caps more than a year of negotiation begun by Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said the bill 'has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions,' warning Trump could impose tariffs 'up to 100%, with no guardrails or oversight, and no expiration.'

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said the bill's loopholes make it 'very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day,' and warned it could give Trump 'unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people.'

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who helped negotiate the tariff language, defended it by saying that if 'Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously.'

Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, called the bill 'a moral issue that requires moral courage,' saying it would 'cripple the Russian war machine and turn the tide toward peace' by targeting the money fueling Russia's war effort.
Some Republicans opposed the bill out of concern that its expanded tariff authority could raise consumer prices ahead of the November midterm elections, according to DW.

facts: The House passed the Russia sanctions bill 262-159 on Wednesday, sending it to President Trump's desk after the Senate passed it 86-11 in August.

The legislation is formally named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, honoring the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who spent over a year negotiating it before his death in July.

The bill sanctions Russian officials, banks and financial institutions, and the 'shadow fleet' of tankers used to move Russian energy, while also reinserting sanctions on Iran's weapons and energy sectors.

It gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and natural gas (such as China and India), with an exemption for countries importing less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports that have taken steps to reduce those imports; some provisions allow tariffs up to 500% on Russian imports.
Vote counts on Democratic support varied by outlet (reported as either 53 or 58 House Democrats voting yes), but a majority of Democrats opposed the bill while seven Republicans voted against it.

Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., broke with party leadership on a Tuesday procedural vote to advance the bill, drawing a public rebuke from Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Trump has said he will sign the bill into law.
ladder.analysis:
The measure is described as the most significant congressional action against Russia since Trump returned to office, aiming to squeeze the Kremlin's war financing through sanctions on officials, banks and energy-linked shipping while also pressuring third countries like China and India that buy Russian oil and gas. Its passage caps more than a year of negotiation begun by Sen. Lindsey Graham, whose death in July gave the bill its name and added symbolic weight to its final push through Congress.

The central tension in the debate was not over sanctioning Russia itself — which drew broad bipartisan backing — but over a provision granting Trump tariff authority to enforce those sanctions. Democratic leaders warned this could hand the president broad, loosely checked power to tariff countries of his choosing, while some Republicans worried the tariffs could raise consumer prices ahead of the midterms. Supporters, including the bill's chief House sponsor, framed the tariff mechanism as essential because sanctions alone have proven easy for Russia to evade in the past.

dem: Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said the bill 'has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions,' warning Trump could impose tariffs 'up to 100%, with no guardrails or oversight, and no expiration.'

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said the bill's loopholes make it 'very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day,' and warned it could give Trump 'unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people.'

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who helped negotiate the tariff language, defended it by saying that if 'Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously.'
rep: Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, called the bill 'a moral issue that requires moral courage,' saying it would 'cripple the Russian war machine and turn the tide toward peace' by targeting the money fueling Russia's war effort.
Some Republicans opposed the bill out of concern that its expanded tariff authority could raise consumer prices ahead of the November midterm elections, according to DW.

ladder.steelman: Even lawmakers who agree Russia's war economy must be squeezed are split by a deeper, cross-partisan question: whether concentrating enforcement power in tariff authority under one president is an acceptable price for tougher sanctions, or a precedent that outlasts the war itself.
ladder.implications: With Trump expected to sign the bill, attention will shift to how — and whether — the administration actually imposes the authorized tariffs on major Russian energy importers like China and India, a decision that could reshape U.S. trade relations with those countries. Democrats' warnings about unchecked tariff power set up potential legal battles if the authority is used beyond its stated Russia-related purpose, while the bill's real-world effect on Putin's war financing and the Ukraine conflict will depend on how aggressively the sanctions and tariffs are enforced.

stories.headline: Canada seeks EU associate membership; Trump threatens tariffs

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: Canadian PM Mark Carney said Thursday he welcomes an invitation for Canada to become the EU's first-ever 'associate member.'
Carney delivered a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday, in her State of the Union address, that she wants to work 'on opening the door' for Canada to become an EU associate member, covering areas like manufacturing and energy.
President Trump said Wednesday that the EU granting Canada associate-member status could be a 'hostile act.'
Trump threatened to impose 'very serious tariffs' or halt trade with Europe if the EU proceeds with granting Canada associate-member status.
Carney told reporters Sunday that Canada is seeking a 'unique alliance' with the EU.
An EU-Canada summit is scheduled for the end of next month.
The EU-Canada summit is to be followed by technical working groups.
Canada earlier this year joined the EU's SAFE defense fund.
The Canada-EU CETA trade deal has been in force for nearly a decade.
CETA has eliminated 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.
A Nanos poll from April found more than four in five Canadians favor stronger EU ties.
The Nanos poll found close to three in five Canadians support Canada joining the EU outright.
Article 49 of the EU treaty makes formal membership for a non-European country legally impossible.
US-Canada trade talks broke down in late August amid an escalating tariff dispute.
Carney imposed counter-tariffs on the US.
EU-Canada bilateral trade totaled about $130bn last year.
US-Canada trade totaled roughly $900bn last year.
The US buys about 70% of Canadian exports.
The push for closer Canada-EU ties comes amid an ongoing US-Canada tariff dispute.
The push for closer Canada-EU ties comes amid broader unease among US allies about the Trump administration's use of trade and territorial threats as leverage.
Trump has repeatedly talked of Canada as a '51st state.'
Trump has applied pressure over Greenland.
Canada and the EU already have deep economic links via CETA.
Canada and the EU already have defense cooperation through SAFE.
Both sides frame the new associate-member push as part of a diversification strategy.
Canada wants to cut reliance on the US market.
The EU wants access to Canadian LNG, critical minerals and defense manufacturing.
Formal EU membership for Canada is legally barred under Article 49.
'Associate member' status would be a novel, undefined category requiring new legal and technical work.
Both Canada and the EU are pursuing closer ties largely as a hedge against unpredictability from Washington.
Each remains far more economically dependent on the US than on each other.
The scheduled EU-Canada summit next month and subsequent technical working groups will determine whether 'associate membership' becomes a defined legal status or remains largely symbolic.
Trump's response to the plan—including his tariff threat—will shape whether this diplomatic courtship translates into concrete trade or defense commitments.

facts: Canadian PM Mark Carney said Thursday he welcomes an invitation for Canada to become the EU's first-ever 'associate member,' delivering a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday, in her State of the Union address, that she wants to work 'on opening the door' for Canada to become an EU associate member, covering areas like manufacturing and energy.
President Trump said Wednesday that the EU granting Canada associate-member status could be a 'hostile act,' and threatened to impose 'very serious tariffs' or halt trade with Europe if it proceeds.
Carney told reporters Sunday that Canada is seeking a 'unique alliance' with the EU; an EU-Canada summit is scheduled for the end of next month, to be followed by technical working groups.
Canada earlier this year joined the EU's SAFE defense fund; the Canada-EU CETA trade deal, in force for nearly a decade, has eliminated 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.

A Nanos poll from April found more than four in five Canadians favor stronger EU ties, and close to three in five support Canada joining the EU outright, though Article 49 of the EU treaty makes formal membership for a non-European country legally impossible.
US-Canada trade talks broke down in late August amid an escalating tariff dispute, with Carney having imposed counter-tariffs on the US.
Trade data: EU-Canada bilateral trade totaled about $130bn last year, versus roughly $900bn in US-Canada trade, with the US buying about 70% of Canadian exports.
ladder.analysis: The push for closer Canada-EU ties comes amid an ongoing US-Canada tariff dispute and broader unease among US allies about the Trump administration's use of trade and territorial threats as leverage, including Trump's repeated talk of Canada as a '51st state' and pressure over Greenland. Canada and the EU already have deep economic links via CETA and defense cooperation through SAFE, and both sides frame the new associate-member push as part of a diversification strategy — Canada wants to cut reliance on the US market, while the EU wants access to Canadian LNG, critical minerals and defense manufacturing. However, formal EU membership for Canada is legally barred under Article 49, so 'associate member' status would be a novel, undefined category requiring new legal and technical work.
ladder.steelman: Both Canada and the EU are pursuing closer ties largely as a hedge against unpredictability from Washington, yet each remains far more economically dependent on the US than on each other — meaning this 'alliance' is best understood as risk diversification rather than a realistic substitute for the US relationship.
ladder.implications: The scheduled EU-Canada summit next month and subsequent technical working groups will determine whether 'associate membership' becomes a defined legal status or remains largely symbolic, while Trump's response to the plan—including his tariff threat—will shape whether this diplomatic courtship translates into concrete trade or defense commitments.

stories.headline: Trump seeks largest-ever Israeli bomb transfer; Congress split

claims.text: The Trump administration has informally notified Congress of a proposed $2.8 billion arms package for Israel.
The proposed arms package would include heavy bombs.
Fox News reports the package includes 20,000 unguided MK-84 2,000lb bombs.
Fox News reports the package includes 20,000 BLU-117 2,000lb precision-guided bombs.
Fox News reports the package includes 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads.
BBC, citing Rep. Gregory Meeks, describes the transfer as involving 40,000 bombs overall.
Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY) is the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Rep. Gregory Meeks said he opposes the sale.
Rep. Gregory Meeks cited unresolved concerns about lawful use of the munitions in populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has publicly said he will work to reject or stop the package.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) has publicly said he will work to reject or stop the package.
Under the Arms Export Control Act, formal notification would let Congress attempt to block the sale via a joint resolution.
Blocking the sale would require a veto-proof two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.
The president may bypass congressional review by declaring an emergency.
In 2024, the Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000lb bombs to Israel over civilian-casualty concerns.
The Trump administration reversed the pause on the 2,000lb bomb shipment after taking office.
In 2025, the Trump administration separately approved an approximately $3 billion sale of 35,500 such bombs by bypassing normal congressional review.
The bombs would be funded largely through the U.S. Foreign Military Financing program.
The U.S. Foreign Military Financing program uses congressionally appropriated taxpayer funds for allied arms purchases.
In July, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) forced a House vote on a bill to cut $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel.
103 Democrats supported the bill to cut $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel.
Rep. Thomas Massie was the only Republican to vote in favor of the bill to cut $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel.
The proposed $2.8 billion package would be one of the largest transfers of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in recent years.
The deal is still in the informal congressional notification stage.

Lawmakers can raise objections to the deal, but they have no binding power to stop it unless the administration proceeds to formal notification and a veto-proof majority in both chambers votes to block it.
In 2024, a similar bomb shipment was paused during the Biden administration over concerns about civilian casualties in densely populated Gaza.
The 2024 bomb shipment pause was reversed once Trump returned to office.
Rep. Gregory Meeks says the deal raises 'grave, unresolved concerns' about lawful use of the munitions in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon.
Rep. Gregory Meeks says the deal reflects Congress's duty to ensure lawful, safeguarded use of U.S.-funded weapons.
Sen. Bernie Sanders called on Congress to reject the package.
Sen. Bernie Sanders accused the administration of 'doubling down' on funding what he termed Israel's actions in Gaza.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen criticized the package's use of taxpayer funds.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen asked 'How is this America First?' regarding the package.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen vowed to work to stop the package.
Rep. Thomas Massie was the sole Republican to support a July amendment cutting $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel.
Both sides broadly affirm support for Israel's security.
Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about how the munitions could be used and about congressional oversight of U.S.-funded weapons sales.
The administration can legally bypass formal review for weapons sales.
Passing a resolution to block the sale would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
Given the precedent of the administration bypassing review for a comparable 2025 sale, the bombs could be transferred regardless of congressional objections.

facts: The Trump administration has informally notified Congress of a proposed $2.8 billion arms package for Israel that would include heavy bombs, according to multiple reports cited by BBC and Fox News.

Fox News reports the package includes 20,000 unguided MK-84 2,000lb bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 2,000lb precision-guided bombs, and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads; BBC, citing Rep. Gregory Meeks, describes the transfer as involving 40,000 bombs overall.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY), ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he opposes the sale, citing unresolved concerns about lawful use of the munitions in populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon.
Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) have publicly said they will work to reject or stop the package.

Under the Arms Export Control Act, formal notification would let Congress attempt to block the sale via a joint resolution, but blocking it would require a veto-proof two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate; the president may also bypass congressional review by declaring an emergency.

In 2024, the Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000lb bombs to Israel over civilian-casualty concerns; the Trump administration reversed that pause after taking office and, in 2025, separately approved an approximately $3 billion sale of 35,500 such bombs by bypassing normal congressional review.
The bombs would be funded largely through the U.S. Foreign Military Financing program, which uses congressionally appropriated taxpayer funds for allied arms purchases.
In July, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) forced a House vote on a bill to cut $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel; 103 Democrats supported it, while Massie was the only Republican to vote in favor.
ladder.analysis: The proposed $2.8 billion package would be one of the largest transfers of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in recent years, building on a similar nearly $3 billion sale earlier in 2025. Because the deal is still in the informal congressional notification stage, lawmakers can raise objections, but they have no binding power to stop it unless the administration proceeds to formal notification and a veto-proof majority in both chambers votes to block it. In 2024, a similar bomb shipment was paused during the Biden administration over concerns about civilian casualties in densely populated Gaza, only to be reversed once Trump returned to office.

dem: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY) says the deal raises 'grave, unresolved concerns' about lawful use of the munitions in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon and reflects Congress's duty to ensure lawful, safeguarded use of U.S.-funded weapons.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) called on Congress to reject the package, accusing the administration of 'doubling down' on funding what he termed Israel's actions in Gaza.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) criticized the package's use of taxpayer funds, asking 'How is this America First?' and vowed to work to stop it.
rep: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) was the sole Republican to support a July amendment cutting $3.3 billion in security aid to Israel.

ladder.steelman: Both sides broadly affirm support for Israel's security, though Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about how the munitions could be used and about congressional oversight of U.S.-funded weapons sales, given that the administration can legally bypass formal review.
ladder.implications: Passing a resolution to block the sale would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers. Given the precedent of the administration bypassing review for a comparable 2025 sale, the bombs could be transferred regardless of congressional objections.

stories.headline: US Congress passes bill allowing 100% tariffs on Russian oil buyers, targeting India and China
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The United States House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation granting President Donald Trump broad authority to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas. The bill, named the 'Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026' after the late senator who died in July, now goes to Trump to be signed into law. It represents the most significant US action against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House.

The legislation empowers the president to apply tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports to the US from the top five purchasers of Russian energy, military equipment, or countries facilitating Russian sanctions evasion. It also allows tariffs of up to 500 percent on Russian imports directly into the US, which totaled $3.8 billion in 2025. Additional provisions include new sanctions on President Vladimir Putin, more than 20 top officials and companies linked to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's 'shadow fleet' of oil tankers used to evade existing sanctions.

China and India, the two largest buyers of Russian crude, are most exposed. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China accounted for 50 percent of Russia's crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37 percent, Turkey at 5 percent, and the European Union at 5 percent. India's reliance is particularly acute: Russia supplied 30.3 percent of India's crude imports in fiscal 2026, worth $40.8 billion out of a total crude import bill of $134.7 billion. In July 2026, Russian crude accounted for more than half of India's imports, far exceeding the combined share of the next six suppliers.

India's Ministry of External Affairs said it was 'monitoring further developments' and remained 'firmly committed to ensuring energy security' for its people. The ministry noted that the issue had been discussed at high levels with US interlocutors in recent months and that India had 'very clearly articulated' the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market. It added that India would take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal told reporters after the bill's passage: 'China and India, you better buy your oil and gas somewhere else.'

Analysts warned of severe consequences for India. Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), called the bill 'a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms.' Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council said the bill could have 'major problematic impacts for India, and at the worst possible time, amid sensitive final-stage trade talks and shaky broader relations.' The US imported about $104 billion of goods from India in 2025, including electronics, pharmaceuticals, machinery, and petroleum products. India's strategic petroleum reserves hold only 9-10 days of net oil imports, and the country imports more than 88 percent of its crude oil, making it highly vulnerable to supply disruptions.

The bill gives countries 180 days to cut Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington, though the president can shorten that deadline. India has saved an estimated $12.6 billion since shifting to Russian crude after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but discounts have narrowed and shipping, insurance, and sanctions risks have risen. Replacing Russian crude would likely mean higher costs and longer shipping routes. Srivastava argued that India should not allow US tariff threats to determine its energy policy and should continue buying Russian oil as long as it remains commercially competitive, while negotiating firmly without granting unilateral trade concessions.

stories.headline: Russian missile and drone attacks injure at least 19 in Ukraine
body: KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian barrage of missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital and surrounding regions injured at least 19 people overnight and into Thursday morning, Ukrainian officials said. The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attacks struck more than 10 locations in the capital, with a 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy among the injured. Ukraine's Air Force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight assault, which involved ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones and decoys, with the main areas targeted being the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.

In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. Apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged, a private residential building was destroyed, and warehouses, a nursery school, cars and garages were damaged at other locations. In Kyiv, a warehouse, office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged in the Dniprovsky district, with additional damage to warehouses and vehicles in the Solomyansky and Darnitsky districts and a non-residential building in the Podilsky district. In the wider Kyiv region, civilian areas and infrastructure were targeted in the Obukhiv, Brovary, Fastiv and Bucha districts, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Administration. A total of 33 sites were damaged, with the worst reported in the Brovary district, where 14 sites were hit, and the Fastiv district, where 10 were damaged; no casualties were reported there.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces hit metallurgical and electronics plants, factories of the military-industrial complex, and energy and transport facilities in the three regions, and that three bulk carriers and a ferry carrying supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk. Separately, a Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday, killing the ship's captain and injuring three crew members, according to Oleh Kiper, the regional head in Odesa. Kiper said the vessel's superstructure and deck were damaged in the morning attack and accused Russia of deliberately targeting Ukrainian ports and civilian merchant vessels.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces carried out overnight strikes against targets in Russia, including an oil refinery in Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, and a military airfield in the Rostov region. He said the operation against the Yaroslavl refinery was conducted jointly by Ukraine's Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the Foreign Intelligence Service, and that the strike on the Rostov airfield damaged an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters. Regional Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said the resulting fire at the refinery had been extinguished. Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in Rostov and cited "good results in the Black Sea," without giving further details.

The attacks come days after U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in a social media post Monday that Russia and Ukraine had mutually agreed to cease attacking each other's energy facilities, strikes that have led to significant supply issues in both countries. In an interview with CBS News on Tuesday, Zelenskyy pushed back on that claim, saying that while an energy truce was discussed during a recent meeting in Kyiv with Trump's representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, he would agree only if Russia ceases its attacks on Ukrainian energy sites. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine is ready to agree to a truce covering attacks on energy infrastructure and the Black Sea, but said he has yet to see any indication that Russia is prepared to do the same. He welcomed U.S. efforts and said active U.S. involvement could make a truce possible, adding that Ukraine was preparing for a meeting between Zelenskyy and Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly this month. "I believe that achieving a truce could be one of the key outcomes of this meeting. It could be a truce covering both the energy sector and the Black Sea — specifically in that combination," he said.

Peace efforts to end Russia's 4 1/2-year full-scale invasion have stalled, with the issue of territorial concessions in eastern Ukraine among the central sticking points. Successive rounds of U.S.-brokered talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, and Ukraine is also seeking security guarantees from partners for a deal. Russian attacks "almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid" last winter, and Ukraine's energy providers now say they are expecting another very tough winter, according to Al Jazeera's Rory Challands reporting from Kyiv. Russia has promised to increase its "mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months," he said.

Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead, with Moscow handing over the remains of 252 people and receiving 23 bodies in a swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported. Ukraine's government agency handling prisoners of war said the bodies of 252 soldiers were received as part of ongoing exchanges and that they will be identified. Ukrainian officials also welcomed the vote in the U.S. House of Representatives on a package of sanctions targeting Russian officials and key sectors of the economy, saying the measures could increase pressure on Moscow and limit the resources available to finance its war effort. The bill was the last undertaking of the late Republican Sen. Lindsay Graham. "It is precisely Sen. Graham's bill, along with other strong sanctions measures taken by our partners against the source of this war, Russia, that represent an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and force Russia to seek peace," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.

Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that a private residential building was destroyed.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that warehouses, a nursery school, cars and garages were damaged at other locations.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that in Kyiv, a warehouse, office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged in the Dniprovsky district.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported additional damage to warehouses and vehicles in the Solomyansky and Darnitsky districts.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that a non-residential building in the Podilsky district was damaged.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Administration, said that in the wider Kyiv region, civilian areas and infrastructure were targeted in the Obukhiv, Brovary, Fastiv and Bucha districts.
Tymur Tkachenko said a total of 33 sites were damaged.
Tymur Tkachenko said the worst reported in the Brovary district, where 14 sites were hit.
Tymur Tkachenko said the Fastiv district, where 10 were damaged.
Tymur Tkachenko said no casualties were reported there.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces hit metallurgical and electronics plants, factories of the military-industrial complex, and energy and transport facilities in the three regions.
Russia's Defense Ministry said three bulk carriers and a ferry carrying supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk.
Oleh Kiper said a Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday.
Oleh Kiper said the attack killed the ship's captain and injured three crew members.
Oleh Kiper said the vessel's superstructure and deck were damaged in the morning attack.
Oleh Kiper accused Russia of deliberately targeting Ukrainian ports and civilian merchant vessels.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces carried out overnight strikes against targets in Russia.
Zelenskyy said the targets included an oil refinery in Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, and a military airfield in the Rostov region.
Zelenskyy said the operation against the Yaroslavl refinery was conducted jointly by Ukraine's Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the Foreign Intelligence Service.
Zelenskyy said the strike on the Rostov airfield damaged an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters.
Regional Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said the resulting fire at the refinery had been extinguished.
Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in Rostov.
Zelenskyy cited 'good results in the Black Sea,' without giving further details.
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in a social media post Monday that Russia and Ukraine had mutually agreed to cease attacking each other's energy facilities.
Trump claimed that strikes have led to significant supply issues in both countries.
In an interview with CBS News on Tuesday, Zelenskyy pushed back on that claim.

Zelenskyy said that while an energy truce was discussed during a recent meeting in Kyiv with Trump's representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, he would agree only if Russia ceases its attacks on Ukrainian energy sites.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine is ready to agree to a truce covering attacks on energy infrastructure and the Black Sea.
Sybiha said he has yet to see any indication that Russia is prepared to do the same.
Sybiha welcomed U.S. efforts and said active U.S. involvement could make a truce possible.
Sybiha added that Ukraine was preparing for a meeting between Zelenskyy and Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly this month.

Sybiha said: 'I believe that achieving a truce could be one of the key outcomes of this meeting. It could be a truce covering both the energy sector and the Black Sea — specifically in that combination.'
Peace efforts to end Russia's 4 1/2-year full-scale invasion have stalled.
The issue of territorial concessions in eastern Ukraine is among the central sticking points.
Successive rounds of U.S.-brokered talks have failed to produce a breakthrough.
Ukraine is also seeking security guarantees from partners for a deal.
Al Jazeera's Rory Challands reported from Kyiv that Russian attacks 'almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid' last winter.
Ukraine's energy providers now say they are expecting another very tough winter, according to Challands.
Russia has promised to increase its 'mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months,' according to Challands.
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead.
Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported that Moscow handed over the remains of 252 people and received 23 bodies in a swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border.
Ukraine's government agency handling prisoners of war said the bodies of 252 soldiers were received as part of ongoing exchanges and that they will be identified.
Ukrainian officials welcomed the vote in the U.S. House of Representatives on a package of sanctions targeting Russian officials and key sectors of the economy.
Ukrainian officials said the measures could increase pressure on Moscow and limit the resources available to finance its war effort.
The bill was the last undertaking of the late Republican Sen. Lindsay Graham.

Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram: 'It is precisely Sen. Graham's bill, along with other strong sanctions measures taken by our partners against the source of this war, Russia, that represent an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and force Russia to seek peace.'

stories.headline: Eight children among 21 killed in Gaza building collapse
body: At least 21 people, including eight children, were killed and 45 others injured when a war-damaged six-storey building collapsed overnight in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, rescuers and medics said. Witnesses told the BBC that the building had been left tilting dangerously after an Israeli strike more than a year ago, yet displaced families had lived inside because they had no other options. The Hamas-run Civil Defence agency initially used bare hands to search for survivors, later joined by UN and Egyptian teams, before ending the operation on Wednesday afternoon.

A woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said the collapse came suddenly in the early hours: 'It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust. Within minutes, there were screams everywhere.' Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building fell 'in a few seconds' and that stones had been falling from it daily, but residents could not find anywhere else to live. Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: 'They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live. This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death.'

Satellite imagery shows the area was targeted early in the war, with damage to the building itself first visible in 2024. The head of the UN Development Programme office in Gaza, Alessandro Mrakic, said the situation was 'tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed.' He warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches, and appealed for machinery, spare parts and oil. The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was 'devastated' and urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries of heavy machinery, tents and other non-food items for displaced people before winter rains. Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups.

According to the UN, an estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas. More than 1.9 million people – about 90% of the territory's population – have been displaced, with 1.2 million currently living in tents or makeshift shelters. The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation remains dire despite a ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to cause casualties and damage. On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources. Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in northern Gaza; the Israeli military said it was not aware of the incident.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable.

stories.headline: US denies visas to Palestinian officials for second consecutive year ahead of UN General Assembly
body: The Trump administration has denied entry visas to a high-level Palestinian delegation, including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, for the second consecutive year, barring them from attending the annual UN General Assembly meeting in New York in person. The State Department announced the decision on Wednesday, citing the Palestinian Authority's failure to meet commitments to seek peace with Israel.

In a statement, the State Department accused the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organization of continuing to pursue legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court, and of paying stipends to families of prisoners convicted of attacks against Israelis. The department said the groups had 'failed to live up to their commitments' and were engaging in 'ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace.' As a result, the United States will 'extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials' in accordance with standing U.S. law.

The move marks the second year in a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York for the UN General Assembly. Last year, Abbas addressed the gathering by video conference. This year, the UN General Assembly is set to vote on a draft resolution on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely, according to two officials familiar with the planned vote. Despite the visa denials, the Palestinians will still be represented at next week's high-level meeting by their diplomats who are already accredited to the United Nations.

The Palestinian Authority's foreign ministry denied the allegations in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an 'unjustified measure' that 'contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region.'

The visa denials are the latest in a series of restrictive measures by the Trump administration, further signaling the close U.S. alliance with Israel, which has faced international isolation over its war in Gaza following the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas. A fragile, U.S.-brokered ceasefire took hold in October, but Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the Palestinian territory. The decision also comes as the Trump administration has launched a campaign to dismantle the ICC, accusing it of trying to unfairly prosecute U.S. and Israeli soldiers. Neither Israel nor the United States are members of the global tribunal. This year's UN General Assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

stories.headline: Energy costs surge amid Iran war, hitting consumers and transport firms
body: Diesel prices surged to an all-time high of about $6.31 a gallon on Wednesday, up more than 70% from a year ago, as the U.S. war with Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, according to AAA. The spike is pinching transportation companies and adding an estimated $1,760 in costs per U.S. household since the conflict began, Moody’s Analytics found. Trucking and rail firms, which rely on diesel, are warning that the record fuel costs are beginning to weigh on earnings and could ripple through the broader economy.

The national average for diesel could hit $6.50 within two days, with states like Michigan, Ohio and Illinois potentially reaching $7, said GasBuddy’s Patrick De Haan. In California, the average gallon of diesel already topped $8. “We’re talking about $6 diesel, but out here, it’s $8 diesel, which is like science fiction,” said Claude Elkins, chief commercial officer of Norfolk Southern, at an industry conference. J.B. Hunt finance chief Brad Delco said the trucking company expects a 5% to 10% earnings drop from the second to third quarter because of higher fuel costs; shares fell more than 13% Wednesday, their worst session since 1983. The Dow Jones Transportation Average closed nearly 3% lower, with J.B. Hunt the biggest decliner.

Consumers face a double hit from rising energy costs and climbing interest rates. The average gallon of gasoline exceeded $4.32 on Tuesday, up 36% from a year ago, and crude oil topped $105 a barrel. Moody’s estimates that $930 of the per‑household bill comes from higher energy prices, $425 from higher interest rates and $405 from increased military spending. The 10‑year Treasury yield jumped to its highest since 2007, pushing the 30‑year fixed mortgage rate above 7% for the first time in over a year. Airfares have risen more than 23% year over year, and the University of Michigan consumer survey found 29% of respondents cited gas prices in September, up from 6% a year earlier. Total credit card debt hit $1.26 trillion in the second quarter, near a record.

The war — now in its seventh month — shows no signs of resolution, leaving energy markets in deep uncertainty. JPMorgan commodities strategists wrote, “We simply don’t know how to model the endgame.” The Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed to through traffic, with daily crossings in the low double digits versus a pre‑war average of more than 120. Energy Secretary Chris Wright assured CNBC that a Saudi pipeline closure would last only a few days, but crude prices have stayed elevated. Retail sales rose 1.2% from July to August despite the price pressures, and the transport sector added $1.9 trillion to the U.S. economy in 2024, more than 6% of enhanced GDP. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates at its Wednesday meeting, with a more than 92% probability priced into fed funds futures, and the majority of Fed Survey respondents expect at least two hikes in the next year.

Economists warn that high diesel costs will inflate expenses for farmers and transporters before hitting consumers at the grocery store. “Ultimately, over some period of time, that’s going to be a drag on the consumer out there,” Norfolk Southern’s Elkins said. Lower‑income households, which spend a larger share of income on energy, are feeling the strain most acutely, contributing to a K‑shaped recovery. The personal savings rate has fallen to levels rarely seen since the Global Financial Crisis, and inflation is again outpacing income growth, leaving consumers with negative real earnings. “Costs have gone up and income growth has gone down, so something has got to give,” said Luke Tilley, chief economist at M&T Bank and Wilmington Trust.

stories.headline: Bank of England holds rates steady despite UK inflation jump to 3.1%
body: The Bank of England left its key interest rate unchanged at 3.75% on Thursday, despite UK inflation rising to 3.1% in August, but signaled that a rate hike was becoming increasingly likely. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold the Bank Rate, with the three dissenters voting for a 25-basis-point increase to 4%. Markets had priced in a 76% chance of a hold, according to LSEG data, but a hike of at least 25 basis points is widely anticipated at the bank's next meeting in November.

The hold marks a divergence from other major central banks. The U.S. Federal Reserve announced a quarter-point hike on Wednesday, its first since 2023, while the European Central Bank announced its second rate hike this year last week. The Bank of Japan is expected to raise its key interest rate at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday.

Data released Wednesday by the Office for National Statistics showed that the UK's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1% in August, its first reading above 3% since March and in line with economists' expectations. The spike was largely driven by rising motor fuel costs, which surged 23% year-on-year. The average price of gasoline rose by 9.1 pence per liter between July and August, the highest since Nov. 2022, while average diesel prices rose by 14.2 pence per liter. Crude oil prices are hovering above $100 a barrel, and the cost of electricity, gas and other household fuels jumped 6% year-on-year in August.

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in a statement that so far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK. "But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2% target," he said. The three dissenting MPC members — Catherine L Mann, Megan Greene and Huw Pill — argued for a hike, pointing to uncertainty arising from the Iran war and the need to get ahead of its potential economic ramifications. Mann said the conflict had "ratcheted up energy prices well above the baseline from the July Report," while Greene cited uncertainty about second-round effects of the war, AI-related supply constraints and the El Niño climate event. Pill said raising rates would send a "clear signal of the MPC's commitment to achieving its price stability mandate amidst the fog of geopolitical conflict and data noise."

As a net energy importer, the UK is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks and is still grappling with a cost-of-living crisis brought on by post-Covid inflation and the Russia-Ukraine war's impact on natural gas supplies. Global inflation concerns, political instability and apprehension about UK fiscal policy have put pressure on British government bonds, known as gilts, this year. Britain has the highest borrowing costs in the G7, with yields on its long-dated 20- and 30-year gilts approaching the 6% mark. Gilt yields fell sharply after the decision was announced, with the benchmark 10-year yield down 8 basis points to 5.2169%, while 30-year gilt yields shed nearly 12 basis points to trade at 5.7415%.

Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note that the bank was "biding its time," noting that the labour market continues to soften while core and services inflation have been relatively resilient since the Middle East conflict started. "So far, the UK economy has largely been insulated from the conflict, aside from higher energy bills. However, the longer the war continues, the harder it is to see that resilience holding," he said. Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at Premier Miton, said the Bank seems more relaxed on inflation risks than its international counterparts, but added: "With the expectation being for a number of hikes through the end of this year in to middle of next, the gilt market may be more susceptible to a move the other way."

Rising costs also add to the pressure on new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has pledged to tackle the cost-of-living burden but is also tasked with balancing the public books and placating the bond market. James Smith, developed markets economist at ING, said in a note that there was "nothing in the latest UK inflation numbers that screams a need to hike interest rates," pointing to food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation, which slipped to 1.1% year-on-year in August, and little sign that the energy shock is broadening out to other parts of the inflation basket. Bogdan Toma, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said gasoline prices at their highest level in nearly four years could signal "an uncertain 'golden quarter' for consumers and retailers," with demand heading into the fourth quarter potentially subdued. Gardner added that his team is watching closely for potential second and third round effects from higher costs, noting that food prices have started to eke upwards after fertilizer costs increased earlier this year, and that AI is an important but often overlooked factor as demand for metals, semiconductors and other supply-chain goods grows. "For now, it is too early to tell if the energy price spike is evolving into a broader inflation shock but fears will be growing. Much still depends on the duration of the war in the Middle East," he said.

James Smith said there was little sign that the energy shock is broadening out to other parts of the inflation basket.
Bogdan Toma, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said gasoline prices at their highest level in nearly four years could signal "an uncertain 'golden quarter' for consumers and retailers."
Bogdan Toma said demand heading into the fourth quarter could be potentially subdued.
Gardner added that his team is watching closely for potential second and third round effects from higher costs.
Gardner noted that food prices have started to eke upwards after fertilizer costs increased earlier this year.
Gardner said that AI is an important but often overlooked factor as demand for metals, semiconductors and other supply-chain goods grows.
Gardner said: "For now, it is too early to tell if the energy price spike is evolving into a broader inflation shock but fears will be growing."
Gardner said: "Much still depends on the duration of the war in the Middle East."

stories.headline: U.S. measles deaths reach highest level in decades as local officials step in amid federal inaction
body: Pennsylvania reported two more measles-related deaths yesterday, bringing the total number of U.S. measles deaths this year to four—the highest annual tally since 1992. The two latest victims were a 40-year-old woman and an 18-year-old. The deaths are part of a growing outbreak that has reached 693 cases across 38 counties, according to state data reported as of Sept. 14.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has disputed the role of measles in the first two deaths this year, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not yet registered any measles-related deaths for 2026. In a post on X, Kennedy said, "CDC will report measles-caused deaths when the National Center for Health Statistics reports measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states." Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, noted that Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News last year that the measles vaccine causes blindness and death, adding, "Could he be more dangerously irresponsible? He should have been fired right there, but he wasn’t. And that’s when he knew: I can say whatever I want with impunity."

With federal guidance no longer considered reliable, local and state officials have taken the lead in defending childhood vaccinations. In Delaware County, Pennsylvania, the health department runs a back-to-school immunization campaign that includes a mobile vaccine clinic—a 33-foot RV—and partnerships with school districts. On a recent "exclusion day," when students without complete immunizations were barred from class, the county vaccinated 42 middle and high school students so they could return to their desks. "We’ve been doing this for a couple of years now, and it’s really effective," said Lora Werner, director of the Delaware County Health Department.

The national context includes a recent executive order signed by President Trump that calls for reducing the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 and splitting the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) shot into three separate injections. Experts noted that no new scientific evidence supports the change and that manufacturers have said they have no plans to reformulate the vaccine. Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said, "Our responsibility is to demonstrate what the science shows and put out a [vaccine] schedule that people can depend upon that is science-based and evidence-based. Measles is a canary in the coal mine and we have to now worry about other vaccine-preventable diseases, which is why the local effort at the state level is so critical."

In response, at least 30 states now report relying on sources other than the CDC—such as the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians—for childhood vaccine guidance. Fifteen states have sued the Trump administration over changes to the vaccine schedule and the dismantling of the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel. Two voluntary regional coalitions have formed: the West Coast Health Alliance (California, Oregon, Washington, Hawaii) and the Northeast Public Health Collaborative (15 states including Connecticut, Maine, New York, Massachusetts). Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of the nonprofit advocacy group 3.14 Action, said, "This is the last thing parents wanted on their back-to-school list, to be confused about the childhood vaccine schedule or to be worried about their child coming home with measles. It’s why so many doctors and health professionals are now stepping up and fighting back against these dangerous actors."
